Four worked examples

What a product manager can hand to Devin, and what comes back

Each example below shows the exact prompt, how long it took, and the real output from one run. Copy a prompt, change the parts in brackets, and try it on your own work.

Everything here uses a demo workspace. The data, interviews, backlog and show titles are synthetic and written for this demo. Nothing comes from Comcast systems.

Overview

Devin supports non-engineering teams, acting like a junior employee

Devin is a junior employee that reads your product, code, docs and data, then returns work you can review: specs, syntheses, analyses and prototypes.

Who it helps

01

Product managers

Define customer problems and product requirements, shape solutions and work with design and engineering to deliver them.

02

Researchers

Build understanding of customers, their needs and behaviors, and bring evidence into product decisions.

03

Analytics

Use data to understand customer and product performance and support evidence-based decisions.

04

Strategists

Explore customer, market and business opportunities and help shape longer-term product direction.

How these teams work with Devin

Ask

Ask Devin and DeepWiki

Ask how the product works in plain language. Answers cite the code and docs they come from, so no IDE is needed.

Hand off

Sessions

Hand off a task from the web app, Slack or Teams. Devin works on its own machine and returns a doc, spreadsheet, deck, prototype, analysis or pull request.

Repeat

Playbooks and schedules

Save a prompt that worked as a Playbook, then run it on a schedule: a weekly readout, a monthly KPI pack, release notes.

Connect

Connected tools

Jira, Confluence, Notion, Google Drive, Slack and your data warehouse through MCP, within the access your admins grant.

How to ask

A good prompt says five things

All four example prompts on this page follow the same shape. None of them needs technical vocabulary.

01

Who you are

Your role, and that you want plain language. Devin then explains instead of jumping to code.

02

What to read

The repo, folder, file or web sources. Name them. Devin works from what you point it to.

03

What to produce

The thinking you want done: a PRD, an analysis, options with a recommendation, a scored backlog.

04

What to send back

The file types you can open and share: PDF, PowerPoint, spreadsheet, HTML.

05

Limits and checks

Limits such as "don’t change the repo." Then ask Devin to list its assumptions at the end, so you know what to check.

Two ways to work with Devin

Ask Devin

A quick question about how something works

Answers in plain language from the code your organization has indexed. Use it when you want to understand, not produce.

Example: "How does Continue Watching decide what to show today?"

Session

A piece of work with something to hand back

Devin runs things, builds files and can keep going while you do something else. All four examples on this page are sessions.

Example: "Write a PRD and build a clickable prototype."

Example 1

PRD and clickable prototype

Devin read 12 customer interviews and the app code, wrote a one-page PRD with quotes traced to participants, and built a three-screen prototype you can click.

Mode
Session
Reads
Interviews, app code, design system
Returns
PRD, HTML prototype, screenshots
Time in our runs
About 6 minutes

Why a session, not Ask Devin: Devin has to build a file, run it and take screenshots. The first half of this task, "how does Continue Watching behave today?", would work as an Ask Devin question on its own.

The prompt

I'm a product manager on the Xfinity Stream app. I'm not an engineer, so keep explanations in plain language.

In the repo EvangelosG/comcast-pm-demo, read the 12 customer interviews in research/interviews and work out how Continue Watching behaves today from the code in app/.

Then:
1. Write a one-page PRD for "continue watching across devices". Cover the problem, target users, user stories with acceptance criteria, success metrics and open questions. Use interview quotes as evidence and say which participant each one came from.
2. Build a clickable mobile prototype of the three key screens as a single HTML file, using the design system in design-system/.

Send me the PRD, the prototype file and a screenshot of each screen. Don't change the repo or open a pull request. Don't wait for me to approve a plan: make sensible assumptions and list them at the end.
I'm a product manager on [product]. I'm not an engineer, so keep explanations in plain language.

In the repo [repo], read the customer interviews in [folder] and work out how [feature] behaves today from the code in [folder].

Then:
1. Write a one-page PRD for "[feature idea]". Cover the problem, target users, user stories with acceptance criteria, success metrics and open questions. Use interview quotes as evidence and say which participant each one came from.
2. Build a clickable prototype of the [number] key screens as a single HTML file, using our design system in [folder].

Send me the PRD, the prototype file and a screenshot of each screen. Don't change the repo or open a pull request. Make sensible assumptions and list them at the end.

What came back

Live prototype

This is the file Devin returned, running inside the page. Tap a card under Continue Watching to walk through the flow.

The PRD below came back in the same message.

What to check before you use it

  • The metric targets are proposals. Devin said so: the workspace has no usage data to set a baseline.
  • Devin counted 10 of 12 participants with the cross-device problem; the backlog says 9. It listed the mismatch as an open question instead of picking one silently.
  • Episode labels and "last watched" times in the prototype are invented placeholders.

Example 2

Data analysis

Devin analyzed 6,000 sign-ups and about 126,000 viewing events to find who left within 30 days, and returned a readout plus a notebook an analyst can rerun.

Mode
Session
Reads
Two CSV files and their README
Returns
One-page readout, notebook
Time in our runs
5 to 11 minutes

Why a session, not Ask Devin: Devin has to load the files, run the analysis and draw charts. Ask Devin answers questions about code; it does not run an analysis.

Tip: for data work, pick the Data Analyst agent. In the agent picker next to the message box, open Mode and choose Data.

The prompt

I'm a product manager for Peacock. I'm not an analyst, so explain the findings in plain language.

In the repo EvangelosG/comcast-pm-demo, use data/subscribers.csv and data/subscriber_events.csv (data/README.md explains the columns).

Find out which sign-up cohorts from the NBA tip-off window (October 21 to 27, 2025) churned within 30 days. Break it down by plan, device, acquisition channel and promo offer, and compare with people who signed up outside the window. Look at viewing behavior too, in case it explains who leaves.

Send me a one-page readout with three charts and three retention recommendations, plus the notebook so an analyst can rerun it. I'll show the readout on a shared screen, so keep the charts large and the text short. State your assumptions and anything in the data I should be cautious about. Don't change the repo or open a pull request. Don't wait for me to approve a plan: make sensible assumptions and list them at the end.
I'm a product manager for [product]. I'm not an analyst, so explain the findings in plain language.

Use [data files or tables] ([where the columns are explained]).

Find out [question, for example which sign-up cohorts churned within 30 days]. Break it down by [dimensions] and compare with [baseline].

Send me a one-page readout with three charts and three recommendations, plus the notebook so an analyst can rerun it. State your assumptions and anything in the data I should be cautious about.

What came back

What to check before you use it

  • The offer was only available inside the tip-off window, so the data cannot fully separate "the week" from "the promo". Devin flagged this itself.
  • The comparison Devin relied on is sign-ups with no offer, inside and outside the window. Check that this is the comparison you would choose.
  • Have an analyst rerun the notebook before a number goes into a decision.

Example 3

Strategy deck from web research

Devin researched seven streaming services on the public web, compared rights, prices and bundles, and built a 10-slide deck with three options and a recommendation.

Mode
Session
Reads
Public web pages
Returns
PowerPoint deck, PDF copy
Time in our runs
14 to 21 minutes

Why a session, not Ask Devin: Devin has to browse the web and build a PowerPoint file. Ask Devin answers from your indexed code, which this task does not use.

The prompt

I'm a strategy lead at Peacock preparing for a leadership review.

Research the US live sports streaming market: Peacock, YouTube TV, ESPN, Fox One, Prime Video, Netflix and Apple TV. Build a short profile of each and a side-by-side comparison of sports rights, prices and bundles.

Then lay out three options for Peacock's 2027 sports offer with pros, cons and risks, and recommend one.

Send me a 10-slide PowerPoint deck, plus a PDF copy. Put the source links in the speaker notes of each slide, give the date you checked each price, and flag anything you could not verify. Don't wait for me to approve a plan: make sensible assumptions and list them at the end.
I'm a [role] at [team] preparing for [meeting].

Research [market]: [list of companies or products]. Build a short profile of each and a side-by-side comparison of [what to compare].

Then lay out three options for [decision] with pros, cons and risks, and recommend one.

Send me a [number]-slide PowerPoint deck, plus a PDF copy. Put the source links in the speaker notes of each slide, give the date you checked each figure, and flag anything you could not verify.

What came back

Sample output, not verified. The figures and the recommendation on these slides were gathered by Devin from public web pages on November 10, 2026 and have not been checked by a person. They are shown to illustrate the format only.

What to check before you use it

  • Every slide carries its source links and price check dates in the speaker notes. Open them.
  • Devin listed what it could not verify, including two prices it could not recheck and subscriber numbers that are third-party estimates.
  • The ranking of options is a judgment, not a financial model. Devin had no internal data.

Make it repeatable

When a session gives you a result you like, such as a deck in the style you want, ask Devin to write up how it made it as a Playbook. Anyone on your team can then attach it to a new session by typing its shortcut, for example !strategy-deck, and naming the topic.

Example 4

Backlog scoring and roadmap

Devin scored 25 epics with RICE, used the interviews as evidence, read the code for dependencies the backlog did not mention, and drafted tickets for the first quarter.

Mode
Session
Reads
Backlog file, interviews, app code
Returns
Spreadsheet, roadmap slide, ticket file
Time in our runs
11 to 13 minutes

Why a session, not Ask Devin: Devin has to produce a spreadsheet, a slide and a ticket file. A single question such as "what does continue watching across devices depend on in the code?" would suit Ask Devin.

The prompt

I'm a product manager on the Xfinity Stream app. I'm not an engineer, so keep explanations in plain language.

In the repo EvangelosG/comcast-pm-demo, score the 25 open epics in backlog/epics.csv on reach, impact, confidence and effort (RICE). Use the customer interviews in research/interviews as evidence for impact and confidence, and read the code in app/ to flag technical dependencies the backlog doesn't mention.

Send me:
1. A spreadsheet of the scored backlog, with a short reason for each impact and confidence score.
2. A now / next / later roadmap as a single PowerPoint slide, plus a PDF copy.
3. Draft tickets for the "now" epics, with user stories and acceptance criteria, in a file I could import into Jira.

Don't change the repo or open a pull request. Don't wait for me to approve a plan: make sensible assumptions and list them at the end.
I'm a product manager on [product]. I'm not an engineer, so keep explanations in plain language.

Score the open epics in [backlog file or Jira project] on reach, impact, confidence and effort (RICE). Use [research source] as evidence for impact and confidence, and read the code in [repo] to flag technical dependencies the backlog doesn't mention.

Send me:
1. A spreadsheet of the scored backlog, with a short reason for each impact and confidence score.
2. A now / next / later roadmap as a single PowerPoint slide, plus a PDF copy.
3. Draft tickets for the "now" epics, with user stories and acceptance criteria.

What came back

What reading the code added: the backlog lists what to build; the code showed what each item depends on. Progress is saved per device, so "remove" and "mark as watched" would only apply to one device until account-level progress ships. Removing a title would also discard its resume point. And the row only clears a title at 95% watched, which explains the backlog note that titles above 90% linger.

What to check before you use it

  • Reach and effort were taken from the backlog as written. If those are wrong, the ranking is wrong.
  • The ticket file is a draft for import. Nothing was created in Jira.

Get started

Try it on your own work

Sessions run in the cloud, so you can start several at once and come back when they finish.

  1. Pick one real taskChoose something you would otherwise spend an afternoon on, where you can judge the result.
  2. Start from a templateOpen the "Template for your own work" tab on the closest example and fill in the brackets.
  3. Start a sessionPaste the prompt into a new Devin session and select the repo it should read, if there is one.
  4. Review, then ask for changesRead the assumptions first. Reply in the same session to change anything, in plain language.

Put it on a schedule

On the first Monday of every month at [time and time zone], start a Devin session in the repo [repo].

The session should read the backlog in [backlog file] and the customer interviews in [folder], score every epic with RICE, and draft a now, next and later roadmap.

Post a short summary and the roadmap slide to the Slack channel [channel]. Don't change the repo.

Where to paste it: open Automations, choose Create automation, then Generate with Devin. Devin drafts the automation and you review it before saving. Jira and Slack triggers need those integrations connected to Devin. Your Devin admin can tell you which ones are on.

Devin is built by Cognition. Demo content is synthetic. Outputs shown are each from a single run on November 10, 2026; times are from two runs of each prompt.
